prompt:
Use case: scientific-educational. Asset: production sprite atlas for Cosmic: A Sea Beneath the Moon. Input image1 is a STYLE reference only: retain the medallion form, palette, grain and physical depiction approach, but create the NEW requested subjects below. Exactly 4 columns by 4 rows, 16 circles total. Regular equal square cells, landscape4:3 ratio for12circles or square for16circles. Aim2048px wide. Every circle diameter84%of its cell, centred, with generous fully transparent gutters; leave allcells complete and separated. No extra cells or objects. Original astronomical chromolithograph with dry-gouache and chalk masses: deep indigo circular fields, feathered warm-ivory light, amber heat, copper/charcoal minerals and restrained teal water. Simplify to broad meaningful structures visible at72px. Fine grain stays in subjects; generous quiet dark space. One thin ivory circular outline. No glossy UI buttons, photographic lens flare, ornamental decoration, humans, machines, text, labels, numerals, formulas or grid lines. Inside each circle the field is opaque; outside circles true alpha transparency. No shadows, rays or fragments beyond circles. Atom/particle diagrams are schematic: tiny compact ivory dots and diffuse electron-probability clouds, never planetary electron orbits; individual nuclei do NOT glow like stars. Exact invisible chemistry is communicated by game names/readings, never by invented diagnostic coloration. All terrestrial worlds have bare mineral terrain; no plants, life or modern continents. Early Moon is pale gray-ivory without familiar dark maria. All Earth cutaways are views of one continuing world.
Strict row-major subjects (left to right, then top to bottom):
1. Expanding stellar ejecta: A broken expanding shell of ivory and copper filaments around a tiny surviving central remnant. Avoid: Explosive ragged radial filaments; keep compact remnant visibly separate.
2. A shock running into gas: An asymmetric bright crescent shock presses into a broad gas cloud, compressing its near edge. Avoid: Interaction at one cloud edge, not a whole spherical explosion.
3. A cooling enriched cloud: A broad irregular cooling gas cloud with faint sparse mineral-coloured particulate suggestion, no bright shock edge. Avoid: Enrichment itself is not uniquely visible; avoid reading coloured flecks as literal atoms.
4. Cooling in a stellar outflow: A thinning warm gas streamer fades outward as a few solid grains appear at its cool far end. Avoid: Cooling transition in an outflow; no snowflakes or Earth weather.
5. An aging lower-mass star: A softly glowing amber star with a slightly extended diffuse edge, alone in the field. Avoid: A different later-generation star; no massive-star explosion or neutron remnant.
6. Fusion in shells around an old core: A stellar cutaway with two broad luminous rings around a small dim old core. Avoid: Only simple shell structure; not the many advanced-burning layers of the massive star.
7. Pulsation of an extended stellar envelope: A large diffuse stellar envelope with two faint offset surface outlines and short alternating radial cues. Avoid: Surface breathing convention, not debris exploding away.
8. An evolved giant with burning shells: An enormous diffuse amber envelope enclosing a compact bright interior visible in one shallow wedge. Avoid: Large tenuous envelope and small core; preserve this giant's identity in later cutaways.
9. Carbon made inside an evolved giant: The same red giant in cutaway, its small inner helium-burning region brought into focus. Avoid: Carbon is hot interior matter, not a charcoal lump or visible chemical stain.
10. Carbon mixed into an outer envelope: The red giant cutaway with two broad convection loops connecting the interior to the outer envelope. Avoid: Transport is visible; do not give carbon an invented black material plume inside plasma.
11. A carbon-bearing stellar wind: The same giant sheds a broad gentle asymmetrical veil, with continuous outward flow rather than explosive shards. Avoid: Slow extended outflow; retain central giant and avoid a supernova shock ring.
12. Carbonaceous grains from a stellar wind: A few dark charcoal irregular grains with ivory edge glints embedded in a fading outward streamer. Avoid: Solid carbonaceous grains, not soot smoke or already assembled rocks.
13. An exposed hot stellar core: A compact hot ivory core sits within a wide retreating faint amber envelope. Avoid: The old envelope remains visible; no explosive remnant shell.
14. A cooling white dwarf: A modest clear ivory stellar disk with a thin soft edge, surrounded by empty space. Avoid: No departing envelope; same remnant identity, exact class relies on label and context.
15. A cloud enriched by a stellar wind: A soft crescent stellar-wind streamer joins a broad irregular interstellar gas cloud. Avoid: A mixing reservoir, not a new star; enrichment chemistry remains label-dependent.
16. Deep mixing after shell pulses: A giant-star cutaway with two broad rising and sinking circulation curls crossing between shell and envelope. Avoid: Stellar envelope geometry; no solid conveyor or chemical colour code.
